hints: Start with the currency idea - a useful energy currency must be able to link energy-releasing reactions to energy-requiring reactions in any part of any cell.
Think about movement inside a cell - what size and solubility properties would let a molecule diffuse quickly through cytoplasm to where energy is needed?
Think about how the energy is released - which part of the ATP molecule is broken off and what type of reaction is this?
Remember the quantity involved - each ATP broken to ADP and Pi releases a small, manageable packet of energy suitable for one reaction.
Think about recycling - what must happen after ATP is used up so the cell does not run out, and what does this tell you about the reaction?
Think about storage versus turnover - is ATP kept as a long-term store or made and broken down very rapidly?
walkthrough:
Why Cells Need a Currency**
Think of ATP as small change. Respiration from glucose releases a lot of energy at once, but most cell reactions need only a little energy at a time. ATP breaks that large amount into small usable packets and can be used in every cell for every energy-requiring process.

Built to Move**
ATP is a small, water-soluble molecule. That matters because cytoplasm is watery. Being small and soluble lets it diffuse quickly from where it is made, for example mitochondria, to where it is needed, for example muscles, ion pumps or ribosomes.

How Energy Is Released**
Energy is released by hydrolysis - addition of water to break the terminal phosphate bond. ATP splits to ADP + Pi. That single step releases $30.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, just enough to drive one reaction like muscle contraction or active transport without wasting a lot as heat.

Reversible and Recycled**
The reaction is easily reversible. ADP + Pi can be rejoined to reform ATP using energy from respiration and photosynthesis. So ATP is an intermediate between energy-yielding and energy-requiring reactions, with a very high turnover and never stored in large amounts.

Final answer: Small and water-soluble so diffuses easily around cell; immediate energy donor by hydrolysis; removal of terminal phosphate to form ADP + Pi releases $30.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$; reaction is reversible so ATP can be reformed; acts as intermediate linking catabolic energy-yielding and anabolic energy-requiring reactions; has high turnover and is not stored.

hints: First recall what a redox dye like methylene blue does during respiration - think about hydrogen released in respiration and colour change when the dye gains hydrogen.
Decide your biological system - what living cells and what respiratory substrate will you mix together with the dye in each tube?
The investigation must be anaerobic - how will you stop atmospheric oxygen reaching the yeast so the dye is the only hydrogen acceptor?
Temperature is your independent variable - how will you set and maintain different temperatures accurately?
Decide what you will actually time or measure with a colorimeter to compare rates between tubes.
Plan a suitable range - how many different temperatures will give you a clear trend from low to denaturing temperatures?
Think about reliability - how many repeats at each temperature and how will you use the data to get a reliable mean?
Think about converting your time measurement into a rate value - what simple calculation links shorter decolourisation time to faster respiration?
Finish by thinking about presentation - what graph of rate against temperature will show the effect clearly?
walkthrough:
The Principle of the Dye**
In respiration, hydrogen is released from substrate and normally passed to oxygen. Methylene blue or DCPIP can act as an artificial hydrogen acceptor instead. When reduced by gaining hydrogen it goes from blue to colourless. Faster respiration means faster release of hydrogen, so faster decolourisation.

Setting Up Anaerobic Yeast Tubes**
Put the same volume and concentration of yeast suspension in each test tube, then add the same volume and concentration of a sugar solution such as glucose, plus the same volume of methylene blue solution. To keep conditions anaerobic, cover each mixture with a thin layer of paraffin oil or seal with a bung. This stops oxygen entering, so any hydrogen must go to the dye.

Controlling Temperature**
Place each tube in a water bath set to a different temperature, for example 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 degrees C. Water baths give stable, even heating. Keep all other variables constant: volumes, concentrations, pH, yeast species and time of mixing.

Measuring Rate**
Start a stopwatch on mixing and record time taken for the blue colour to disappear completely. For more precision, use a colorimeter to follow decrease in absorbance. Shorter time means faster respiration.

Repeats, Rate Calculation and Graph**
Repeat each temperature at least twice more to check reliability and calculate a mean time. Calculate rate as $1/\text{time}$. A larger value means a faster rate. Then plot rate of respiration on the y-axis against temperature on the x-axis to show increase to an optimum due to more kinetic energy and enzyme activity, then fall due to denaturation.

Final answer: Methylene blue/DCPIP acts as hydrogen acceptor and is decolourised when reduced; mix yeast suspension with named sugar solution and dye; exclude oxygen with oil layer or bung; incubate in water baths at set temperatures; measure time taken to become colourless or use colorimeter; test at least 5 temperatures; repeat at least twice more and calculate means; calculate rate as $1/\text{time}$; plot rate of respiration against temperature.
